newsitem.title: USA: TWA faces uphill battle to return to profitability.
newsitem.headline: TWA faces uphill battle to return to profitability.

text.p: A year after the crash of Flight 800, Trans World Airlines is still struggling to return to financial health, and industry analysts say time may be running out for the once-proud airline.
Earnings at the airline have plummeted and there is growing concern on Wall Street that TWA needs to act quickly if it is to remain in business.
"Time is not on TWA's side. The time for swift, decisive action is today, not tomorrow," said Samuel Buttrick, an airline analyst with PaineWebber.

Since the Paris-bound flight exploded and crashed off New York's Long Island on July 17, 1996, killing all 230 people on board, the airline has whittled away at its cash reserves and struggled with management turnover. It also has received a warning from its auditors indicating the company would have trouble surviving under current conditions.

What is more, TWA appears to have missed out on the airline industry's recent boom cycle, which some analysts believe has reached its peak and may be drawing to a close. Airlines, like other cyclical industries, are especially sensitive to fluctuations in the economy.
TWA's stock is trading near $6.50 a share on the American Stock Exchange, down from the low $20s in the months before the crash.
"The company is doing poorly, but they are doing an excellent job with PR. But I don't know how long they can maintain this," said Stephen Klein, an analyst with Standard & Poor's Equity Group.
Klein said the crash of the Paris-bound flight came at an already difficult time for the airline.
"If they hadn't had that crash, they'd still be doing just as bad," he said.
After filing for bankruptcy protection twice in five years, TWA had finally returned to profitability when last year's crash occurred.
Less than 12 hours before the Paris-bound Boeing 747 exploded, TWA had reported strong second-quarter earnings and was predicting good results for the rest of the year.
That forecast never came true. The crash "distracted management's attention from core operating issues and led to lost bookings and revenues," TWA said.

Customers shied away from the airline just as it was aggressively expanding capacity and flight schedules. The lost bookings added to other problems, such as rising fuel costs and scheduling and maintenance woes.

The airline has lost money ever since, in sharp contrast to the record profits enjoyed by its peers. The financial losses are expected to continue when TWA reports its earnings for the second quarter ending June 30.

This year's third quarter, which will show if TWA has managed to capitalise on the typically strong summer travel demand, will offer the clearest indication yet of whether the company is moving toward profitability, analysts said.
"I don't think it would be hyperbole to say that the third quarter is a make or break quarter," said Brian Harris, an airline analyst with Lehman Brothers.

In a recent filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, TWA said "a substantial improvement in its operating profits is necessary for TWA to maintain adequate liquidity to meet its obligations throughout the remainder of 1997."

To survive long-term, analysts say, TWA must upgrade its fleet, reduce its work force and attract more high-paying business customers -- all before the industry's next downturn makes a recovery impossible.

The airline has worked to address those issues, but "the one thing we can't do is control the calendar," said Mark Abels, a spokesman for TWA. "We're doing everything we can to achieve sustainable profitability."

In the past six months, TWA has restructured its New York operations, launched a new advertising campaign and replaced some of its older planes. The average age of TWA's fleet, now about 17.8 years, will shrink to 16.7 years by year-end. But that is still much older than the industry average of 11.9 years.
TWA has also worked to improve its on-time performance, which will help its bid to attract customers.
But industry analysts are only partially impressed.
"On-time performance is nifty, but profits are even better," PaineWebber's Buttrick said.
The cause of the crash has yet to be conclusively determined. While investigators know an explosion in the Boeing 747's centre fuel tank caused the disintegration of the plane, they do not know why.

In an effort to solve the mystery of the disaster, investigators on Monday planned to send an instrument-packed 747 on a test flight from New York's John F. Kennedy airport to retrace the path of the doomed plane.
